md:
### Complications of endocarditis at a glance

| Complication | How often | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Symptomatic cerebrovascular event | Up to 35% (silent lesions up to 80%) | Cerebral MRI (CT if MRI not possible) when suspected; thrombolysis not recommended (III C); thrombectomy may be considered (IIb C); continue anticoagulation with a pre-existing indication |
| Infective (mycotic) aneurysm | 9% (angiography series) to 32% of left-sided IE (CTA series) | CT or MR angiography (I B); DSA is the gold standard; treat large, growing or ruptured aneurysms (I C); endovascular treatment allows cardiac surgery the same day, clipping often needs a 2-week delay |
| Splenic infarct or abscess | Infarcts about 20%; up to 5% progress to abscess | Antibiotics; splenectomy for a large abscess, usually before valve surgery; vaccinate afterwards |
| Pericarditis | 19% of aortic IE (usually with ring abscess); 12% of mitral IE | Look for extension from a root aneurysm or ring abscess |
| Conduction disturbance | 11.5% at diagnosis (third-degree 2.8%) | New AV block from abscess: urgent surgery; epicardial pacing at operation with a predictor of persistence (IIa C); 12.8% needed a pacemaker after surgery |
| Spondylodiscitis | 2 to 10% of IE (osteoarticular infection 6 to 8%) | MRI or PET/CT (I C); more than 6 weeks of antibiotics for S. aureus, Candida, severe destruction or abscess (IIa C); does not contraindicate urgent cardiac surgery |
| Acute renal failure | Almost 18% (EURO-ENDO); dialysis 6%, with about 40% mortality | Avoid nephrotoxins, monitor drug levels and creatinine, minimise contrast; should not delay cardiac surgery |

Source: summarised from ESC 2023 section 9 (Recommendation Tables 13 to 15) as given in this section.
anchor: Avoid nephrotoxins where possible; monitor aminoglycoside and vancomycin levels and creatinine

md:
### Prosthetic, TAVI and TPVI endocarditis compared

| | Surgical prosthetic valve | After TAVI | After TPVI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incidence | 0.3 to 1.2% per patient-year (1 to 6% of recipients) | 0.3 to 1.9 per 100 patient-years; highest in the first year | 1.6 to 4.0 per 100 patient-years |
| Main organisms | Peri-operative: S. aureus, S. epidermidis, nosocomial organisms; late: as native valve IE | Enterococci and S. aureus, then streptococci and CoNS | S. aureus and oral streptococci |
| Imaging | Echo and blood cultures each about 60% sensitive; a new periprosthetic leak is a major criterion; FDG-PET/CT adds sensitivity | No vegetation on TOE in 38 to 60%; PET/CT or CTA changed the diagnosis in 33% | ICE and FDG-PET/CT if TTE/TOE negative; new moderate or severe prosthetic stenosis in one-third to one-half |
| Mortality | In-hospital 20 to 40% | In-hospital or 30-day 16 to 36%; 41 to 59% at 1 year | IE-related 0 to 11% |
| Surgery | Early PVE (within 6 months): new valve and complete debridement (I C); uncomplicated non-staphylococcal late PVE can be managed conservatively | Done in about 20%; may be recommended with abscess or fistula if risk is not prohibitive | Surgical valve replacement in 26 to 56% |
| Healed IE with valve dysfunction | — | Valve-in-valve at least 1 to 3 months after the episode, after a negative TOE | Valve-in-valve at least 1 to 3 months after antibiotics; urgent balloon dilatation for severe stenosis |

Source: summarised from ESC 2023 sections 12.1 and 12.3 as given in this section.
anchor: lower than after TAVI (younger, fewer co-morbidities)

md:
### Which aortic stenosis number to trust

| Measure | Strength | Pitfall |
|---|---|---|
| Peak velocity | Strongest single predictor of outcome; most reproducible | Flow dependent: under-calls with a low stroke volume (poor LV, small cavity, AF, significant MR), over-calls in high flow (AR, anaemia, sepsis); beam misalignment only underestimates |
| Mean gradient | ESC/EACTS 2025: the most reliable parameter | Under 40 mmHg with an area of 1 cm² or less: low-flow or normal-flow low-gradient AS, which needs confirmation |
| Valve area (continuity) | Less flow dependent | Most error-prone: squares the LVOT diameter and assumes a circular outflow tract; an area under 1.0 cm² alone over-calls severe AS |
| Dimensionless index | Avoids the LVOT diameter error; under 0.25 makes severe AS highly likely | — |
| CT calcium score | Confirms true severe AS in low flow | Interpret with caution in bicuspid valves, amyloidosis and fibrotic stenosis |

Source: summarised from "Which number matters most" in this section and ESC/EACTS 2025 section 8 (Aortic stenosis part 1, this tab).
anchor: Once stenosis is severe, symptoms and LV function decide timing more than either number.

md:
### Severe aortic stenosis: what changed from 2021 to 2025

| Recommendation | ESC/EACTS 2021 | ESC/EACTS 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| TAVI | 75 years or over, or STS-PROM/EuroSCORE II over 8% | 70 years or over with a tricuspid valve and suitable anatomy (I A) |
| SAVR | Under 75 years and surgical risk under 4% | Under 70 years and low surgical risk (I B) |
| Non-transfemoral TAVI | IIb C | IIa B |
| Low-flow, low-gradient AS, reduced LVEF | Flow reserve required | Flow reserve no longer required (I B) |
| Low-flow, low-gradient AS, preserved LVEF | IIa C | IIa B |
| Asymptomatic severe AS, LV function | LVEF under 55%: IIa | LVEF under 50%: I B; LVEF under 55% moved into the IIa list |

Source: summarised from the 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline's changes from 2021 (Table 4) as given in this section.
